card_quote: A fact I can turn into a quiz question or win an argument with, and sources matter when the quizmaster is challenged. I keep a notebook of questions that caught my team out.
how_read: Cover to cover in twenty-minute bursts over a few evenings with a pencil and the notebook beside me. I ticked my honest guesses, copied out the ones that would make a quiz question, and used the contents page to find my way back. Got to the end of Round 8 within the week and put it down there for the time being.

w1_friction.note: Don't be the one who repeats it? Mate, I've been repeating the Eskimo snow words since 1994.
w1_friction.quote: Don’t be the one at the table who repeats it.

w1_friction.note: Contents says Round 5 starts on 101. It starts on 103. Out by two from there on.
You can't use DISPUTED in a quiz round, the room would riot. Murphy needs a ruling.
w1_friction.quote: Who first said it, and in what words, is not settled.

w1_friction.note: That's Hanlon's razor again, same answer as the page before with a different name on it.

w1_friction.quote: Did Benjamin Franklin fly a kite in a thunderstorm?

w1_friction.note: Verdict says TRUE and the text says he never flew it. One line of source, Wikipedia. A quizmaster would be torn apart.

w1_friction.note: If nobody can find a record, I'd have said folklore. DISPUTED for a story with no proof seems soft.

w1_best.why: Trumpeters on a train. That is a proper quiz question and the answer sounds made up but isn't.
The spelling is deliberate. Made me laugh and I've used it already.
Worn pages in the log tables. Notebook material.
The bike shed committee never met. I've quoted that one in meetings for years.
Toast and a physics paper with a prize. Perfect pub fact.

w1_flat.why: Same answer as Hanlon, only the name changes.
Laffer for the second time, nothing new.
Wald again straight after the bomber one.
Fourier transforms in a trivia book.
Four paragraphs of critics for a number I'd never be asked.

w1_review.headline: Good for the notebook, the hedging aside
w1_review.body: I've lifted about thirty questions from this for the Thursday quiz and even the ones I got right taught me something. The verdict pages are properly sourced and the Tell someone line is exactly what a quizmaster wants. It loses a point for pairs of stories that cover the same ground, and for a couple of pages that look put in by someone else, with a verdict that contradicts its own text. Bottom line: buy it for the quiz team, but check the Franklin page yourself.

w2_review_first: It's a good source of questions, I've nicked plenty for my notebook. Too many answers come out as 'it's complicated', and a couple of pages look like they were put in by a different author. Decent paperback though.

w2_lost.why: Napoleon straight after Hanlon, felt like the same page twice.
Wald for the second time in a row.
Uncertainty principle, too much physics for a pub quiz.

w2_read_aloud.why: Nobody expects the trumpeters to be real.
The committee never met. Everyone's been in that meeting.
Toast always gets a laugh, and there's a prize behind it.
The spelling's deliberate, people want to correct it and then realise.
Six downloads, two of them her own lawyers. Great last line.

w2_cut.why: Napoleon is the same answer as Hanlon.
Wald twice, one good page would do.
The Franklin page with the wrong number and a verdict that fights its own text.

w2_book2: If the next one hedges every answer into mush, or has more pages where the verdict contradicts the text, I'm out.
